verses.text: When a man takes a wife and marries her, then it shall be, if she finds no favor in his eyes, because he has found some unseemly thing in her, that he shall write her a bill of divorce, and put it in her hand, and send her out of his house.
When she has departed out of his house, she may go and be another man’s wife.
If the latter husband hates her, and write her a bill of divorce, and puts it in her hand, and sends her out of his house; or if the latter husband die, who took her to be his wife;

her former husband, who sent her away, may not take her again to be his wife, after that she is defiled; for that is abomination before Yahweh. You shall not cause the land to sin, which Yahweh your God gives you for an inheritance.
When a man takes a new wife, he shall not go out in the army, neither shall he be assigned any business. He shall be free at home one year, and shall cheer his wife whom he has taken.
No man shall take the mill or the upper millstone as a pledge; for he takes a life in pledge.
If a man is found stealing any of his brothers of the children of Israel, and he deals with him as a slave, or sells him; then that thief shall die. So you shall remove the evil from among you.
Be careful in the plague of leprosy, that you observe diligently, and do according to all that the priests the Levites teach you. As I commanded them, so you shall observe to do.
Remember what Yahweh your God did to Miriam, by the way as you came out of Egypt.
When you lend your neighbor any kind of loan, you shall not go into his house to get his pledge.
You shall stand outside, and the man to whom you lend shall bring the pledge outside to you.
If he is a poor man, you shall not sleep with his pledge.
You shall surely restore to him the pledge when the sun goes down, that he may sleep in his garment, and bless you. It shall be righteousness to you before Yahweh your God.
You shall not oppress a hired servant who is poor and needy, whether he is one of your brothers, or one of the foreigners who are in your land within your gates.
In his day you shall give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down on it; for he is poor, and sets his heart on it; lest he cry against you to Yahweh, and it be sin to you.
The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, neither shall the children be put to death for the fathers. Every man shall be put to death for his own sin.
You shall not deprive the foreigner or the fatherless of justice, nor take a widow’s clothing in pledge;
but you shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt, and Yahweh your God redeemed you there. Therefore I command you to do this thing.

When you reap your harvest in your field, and have forgotten a sheaf in the field, you shall not go again to get it. It shall be for the foreigner, for the fatherless, and for the widow; that Yahweh your God may bless you in all the work of your hands.
When you beat your olive tree, you shall not go over the boughs again. It shall be for the foreigner, for the fatherless, and for the widow.
When you harvest your vineyard, you shall not glean it after yourselves. It shall be for the foreigner, for the fatherless, and for the widow.
You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt. Therefore I command you to do this thing.

footnotes.content: Moses allows divorce here, and I notice he doesn't hide the heart's trouble—'unseemly thing,' some broken fit. This isn't endorsing hard hearts but rather containing the harm when love has died. The requirement of a written bill protects the woman from abuse and abandonment. Even in permitting what's lawful, God builds in mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The divorced woman may choose a new life, a new marriage—not shamed into servitude or destitution by the law. I see the Lord's hand even in the permission: she is not condemned to endure or disappear, but given the liberty to begin again.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A second marriage may also fail—either by his hatred or his death. Life is fragile, and the law does not pretend otherwise. The straightforward recital of hard truths ('hates her,' 'die') reminds us that even in a covenant people, sorrow is real.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A man may not take back a wife after she has married another—even if he now regrets it. This boundary protects her dignity and prevents her from becoming a possession to reclaim. The rule is strict because she is not an object to be traded; the ground of the law is her honor and his accountability.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A newlywed man is excused from military service and public business for a whole year—to cherish his wife. What a gift! One year to know her, to be fully present. This is no mere sentiment; it is law. The Lord Himself insists that love needs time and undivided devotion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No creditor may take the millstones—the very tool by which a family grinds its daily bread. To seize them is to steal the means of survival. The law knows that some things are not for sale, no matter the debt. A person's ability to feed themselves must not be sacrificed to repay money.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Stealing a brother and selling him into slavery brings the death penalty—such is the gravity of theft of a person's freedom. The sin is not merely commerce but violence against kinship itself. 'Remove the evil'—the harsh words remind me that some betrayals cut so deep that the community must respond with finality.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Leprosy is a plague that separates, and the people must attend carefully to what the priests teach. Humility here is the heart: I will listen, learn, and obey the expert voice. There is no room for folk remedy or pride; disease demands submission to knowledge and instruction.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Remember Miriam, struck with leprosy when she spoke against Moses on the journey. That plague on her body was not her undoing—the Lord healed her—but a sign that even great servants answer to His word. She is a living memory: rebellion carries a cost, and restoration comes through His mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When you lend, you shall not enter your neighbor's house to seize what he owes you as security. The boundary is clear: the debt is his responsibility, but you may not invade his home to claim it. Respect for the sanctuary of another's dwelling runs deep in the law.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You stand outside; he brings the pledge out to you. This simple choreography preserves both dignity and distance. You do not ransack; he is not humiliated in his own home before his family. Even in the enforcement of debt, courtesy matters.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If he is poor, you shall not sleep with his pledge—do not keep the security overnight. The poor man's hardship is real, and you must not compound it by taking the very thing that keeps him warm. Compassion is not optional; it is the law.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Restore the pledge when the sun goes down, that he may sleep in his garment and bless you. I hear the tenderness here: let him rest tonight, clothed and grateful. His blessing becomes your righteousness before the Lord—kindness is not charity, it is covenant obedience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A hired servant who is poor and needy—whether brother or foreigner—must not be oppressed. The law does not distinguish in their protection; both stand in the same need and are owed the same justice. Mercy levels the field.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pay his wages the same day, before sunset—he is poor and his heart is fixed on that pay to buy food. To delay or withhold is to cause him to cry out to the Lord against you, and that cry becomes your sin. The Lord hears the laborer's voice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fathers shall not die for children, nor children for fathers—every person is accountable only for his own sin. This breaks the cycle of blood guilt and inherited curse. It is a proclamation of individual moral weight: you answer for yourself alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Do not deprive the foreigner, the fatherless, the widow—do not take the widow's garment as pledge. These are the voices with no strength to protest, no family to defend them. The law speaks for them, and by it, God binds you to care.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Remember you were a slave in Egypt; the Lord redeemed you. Your own deliverance is the reason you must show mercy. You have tasted captivity and the sweetness of freedom; therefore, you must be the voice and hand for those still trapped.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When you harvest and forget a sheaf in the field, do not return for it—leave it for the foreigner, fatherless, widow. This is not loss; it is intention written into the harvest itself. The Lord builds provision for the vulnerable into the very fabric of your work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When you beat your olive tree for oil, do not go over the boughs again. Leave the gleanings for those without. The beauty of the law is its simplicity: once you have taken what you came for, you stop; the rest belongs to mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When you harvest your vineyard, do not glean after yourselves—do not strip it bare for greed. Leave fruit on the vine for those who have nothing. This is the third gleanings law, and the repetition tells me: the Lord cares deeply that we leave room for the poor at every harvest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Remember you were a slave in Egypt—and here the law circles back to this anchor one final time. Looking back from where we stand now, I see how the Lord used that bondage to teach His people compassion. We have known captivity, and by that memory, we are bound to free others from theirs. Readers today hear an echo in the Lord's constant return to what He has already done: He frees us first, then asks us to remember, then commands us to act.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
